analysis.one_liner: Bars meatpackers from owning, feeding, or controlling livestock bound for their own slaughterhouses.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with bipartisan farm-state backing, never got a committee vote and died when the 107th Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: Large meatpacking companies increasingly own or contract the cattle and hogs they slaughter, so they buy from themselves instead of competing in the open market for farmers' animals. This bill would amend a 1921 law to make that practice illegal, with carve-outs for farmer-owned cooperatives and very small packers. It gave hog packers 18 months to unwind existing arrangements and other packers up to 180 days. The Senate Agriculture Committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Independent cattle ranchers and hog farmers, who would once again be able to sell their animals into an open market instead of competing against the packer's own captive supply of livestock. Producer-owned cooperatives and small producer-owned packers were explicitly exempted, so farmer-owned processing could continue.

how_it_helps.text: Makes it unlawful for a packer to own, feed, or control livestock it intends to slaughter, restoring open-market competition for farmers' animals.
Applies the ban to companies that control a packer indirectly or through common ownership, closing the obvious loophole of doing it through a subsidiary.
Exempts farmer-owned cooperatives and small producer-owned packers that slaughter under 2% of a livestock type, so the ban targets the large integrated packers rather than farmer-owned businesses.
Gives hog packers 18 months after enactment to unwind existing ownership arrangements, so the transition would not be abrupt.

analysis.who_pays: The large meatpacking companies — firms like the major beef and pork packers — that rely on owning or contracting their own livestock supply. They would have to buy animals on the open market, potentially paying farmers more per animal and losing control over supply. Some economists and packers argued consumers could face somewhat higher meat prices if integration efficiencies are lost.

drawbacks.text: Packers and some economists argue that vertical integration improves efficiency, quality control, and consistency of supply, and that a ban could raise costs that get passed to consumers.

The ban covers livestock owned, fed, or controlled 'for more than 14 days prior to slaughter,' and enforcement would depend on the Secretary of Agriculture policing indirect control through affiliated companies — a rule easy in principle, harder in practice.
The bill does not address packer marketing contracts and other captive-supply arrangements short of ownership and control, so some integration practices would continue.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For farmers facing shrinking market access, the upside is real: an open market with more buyers bidding for their animals. The costs are efficiency losses in the integrated packing system and possible modest consumer price effects, which packers emphasized and supporters disputed. The main design weakness is that it targets ownership and control while leaving other captive-supply tools available, and its practical reach depends on rigorous enforcement of the indirect-control language.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced with two Democratic and two Republican senators behind it, sent to the Senate Agriculture Committee, and never brought up for a vote — it died there when the Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Senator Tim Johnson of South Dakota introduced the bill on January 22, 2001, joined by Senators Grassley, Thomas, and Daschle — a bipartisan, farm-state group.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry on the day it was introduced.
The committee never held a markup or reported the bill, and the full Senate never voted on it; the only further action in the record was the sponsor's introductory remarks in March 2001.
The bill expired when the 107th Congress ended on January 3, 2003, and packer ownership of livestock remained lawful.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The large meatpacking companies, which kept the ability to own, feed, and control their own slaughter-bound livestock without facing a ban. Farmers who wanted an open market got nothing from this Congress.

for.name: Tim Johnson
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate.

against.name: Senate Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a markup or reported it out during the two-year Congress.

against.name: Large meatpacking industry
against.role: Beef and pork packers with vertically integrated livestock operations
against.what_they_did: Opposed a packer ownership ban, arguing integration lowers costs and improves quality control.

sides.party_line_note: The four senators behind the bill split evenly, two Democrats and two Republicans, all from farm states; the bill's failure to get a committee vote cannot be attributed to either party bloc alone.

industries.note: The bill would bar packers from owning, feeding, or controlling the livestock they slaughter, forcing them to buy on the open market and likely raising the prices they pay farmers. Packagers argued integration keeps costs down; for farmers, packer-owned captive supply means fewer open-market buyers.

industries.industry: Independent cattle ranchers and hog farmers
industries.note: Farmers would gain more open-market buyers for their animals instead of competing against a packer's own captive supply. This is the bill's core purpose.

industries.industry: Farmer-owned cooperatives and small producer-owned packers
industries.note: The bill explicitly exempted cooperatives majority-owned by member producers and producer-owned packers slaughtering under 2% of a livestock type, locking in farmer-owned processing as a legal alternative to packer integration.
